title: Assessing the Validity of Health Messages Used by the Saudi Public in WhatsApp
screen_reason: Content analysis of 326 Arabic-language health WhatsApp messages, each independently reviewed by two board-certified physicians and classified as valid, inaccurate (mixed correct and incorrect) or invalid, i.e. explicit truth/falsity coding against expert evidence review. The paper reports the share of items that were inaccurate or invalid (86%, ~280/326) and the share invalid (63.2%, 206/326), both with a stated denominator.

estimates.measure_type: % of health-related WhatsApp messages judged by physician reviewers to be inaccurate or invalid (i.e. not valid)
estimates.value_raw: Around 280 (86%) -- invalid with or without potential risk (63.2%) plus inaccurate (22.4%); only 14.4% valid
estimates.denominator: 326 Arabic-language health-related WhatsApp messages contributed by 282 first preparatory-year students at King Saud University, Riyadh (messages they or a relative had recently read), after excluding exact duplicates and non-health messages
estimates.definition: A message counted in the numerator if physician reviewers classified it as 'inaccurate' (contains mixed correct and incorrect information) or 'invalid' (with or without potential health risk); the complement is 'valid - contains correct information supported by evidence'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Validity (Accuracy and safety) has four categories: Valid-contains correct information supported by evidence; inaccurate-contains mixed information (correct and incorrect); invalid with no potential health risk; or Invalid with potential health risk."
estimates.source_quote: Around 280 (86%) of the studied messages were either invalid with or without potential risk (63.2%) or inaccurate (22.4%), and only 14.4% were valid (Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 69; also Abstract (Results) and Table 2 total row
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four board-certified family medicine or internal medicine consultants; each message independently reviewed for accuracy by two of them 'based on available scientific evidence', with disagreements resolved by consensus of the other two, who were blinded to the first pair's decision. The paper states explicitly: 'Inter-rater reliability with Kappa was not calculated.'
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were requested to share up to three health-related WhatsApp messages that they had recently read. Examples of such messages are the benefit of stem cells or different herbs for certain diseases and risk factors or causes for diseases and ailments.
estimates.notes: The 86% is stated verbatim by the authors (not a sum I computed), so it is R8-keepable. Small internal arithmetic inconsistency to flag: Table 2's counts give 206 + 73 = 279, while the text says 'Around 280 (86%)' and 63.2% + 22.4% = 85.6%. Broad definition variant (inaccurate OR invalid). Sample is not population-representative: messages are whatever a convenience set of university preparatory-year students chose to submit, so the topic mix is uncontrolled.

estimates.measure_type: % of health-related WhatsApp messages judged invalid (invalid with or without potential health risk), the stricter falsity category
estimates.value_raw: 206 (63.2%) invalid and invalid with potential risk, of 326 (100%)
estimates.denominator: 326 Arabic-language health-related WhatsApp messages contributed by 282 first preparatory-year students at King Saud University, Riyadh, after excluding exact duplicates and non-health messages
estimates.definition: A message counted in the numerator if physician reviewers classified it as 'invalid with no potential health risk' or 'invalid with potential health risk'; excludes the 'inaccurate' (mixed correct and incorrect) category
estimates.misinfo_def: "Validity (Accuracy and safety) has four categories: Valid-contains correct information supported by evidence; inaccurate-contains mixed information (correct and incorrect); invalid with no potential health risk; or Invalid with potential health risk."
estimates.source_quote: Around 280 (86%) of the studied messages were either invalid with or without potential risk (63.2%) or inaccurate (22.4%), and only 14.4% were valid (Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 69; the same counts appear in Table 2, p. 71 (total row: Valid 47 (14.4%), Inaccurate 73 (22.4%), Invalid and Invalid With Potential Risk 206 (63.2%), Total 326 (100%))
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two of four board-certified family/internal medicine consultants reviewed each message independently against available scientific evidence; disagreements adjudicated by the other two, blinded. Kappa not calculated.
estimates.moderator_quote: Each message was independently reviewed for accuracy by two reviewers based on available scientific evidence. Any disagreement between the two independent reviewers was resolved by the other two reviewers (through consensus), who were blinded to the decision of the first reviewers.
estimates.notes: Stricter definition variant of the 86% row in the same country x platform cell: fully invalid messages only, excluding the 'inaccurate/mixed' category. Both 206 and 63.2% are printed verbatim in Table 2 and in the Results text.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) Source-credibility distribution (Table 1: unknown source 273 = 83.7%; known but unqualified person 27 = 8.3%; qualified person 19 = 5.8%; trusted scientific body 7 = 2.1%). This is a provenance measure -- 'unknown source' is not the same as an untrustworthy-source classification against a reliability list -- so I judged it out of scope for CONTENT rather than coding it as a source-level prevalence. An adjudicator may disagree. (2) Validity BY source credibility (Table 2: unknown-source messages 186/273 = 68.1% invalid; unqualified persons 17/27 = 63%; qualified/trusted 3 = 11.5% invalid; 'All scientific authorities' messages were valid and safe (100%)'). These are source-credibility subgroups, not the paper's headline prevalence. (3) 'Furthermore, 12% of them posed a potential health risk' (Discussion): the referent of 'them' is ambiguous (all messages, or the unknown-source subset described in the same sentence), and the invalid-with-risk vs invalid-without-risk split lives only in Figure 1, whose numbers are not in the extracted text; so this stricter variant is not R8-safe. (4) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES an adjudicator should see: the Results text says 'the 237 messages authored by an unknown source' while Tables 1 and 2 both say 273 (apparent digit transposition); the Abstract says 'Only 26 messages (8%) of the total were written by trusted scientific sources' whereas Table 1 gives 7 (2.1%) trusted scientific and 19 (5.8%) qualified persons, i.e. 26 = qualified + trusted, not trusted alone; Table 2's 'Qualified person and trusted scientific' row totals 19 (100%) although its cells are 19 + 4 + 3 = 26. None of these affect the two extracted rows, whose denominator (326) is consistent everywhere.

rob.design: Descriptive analytical cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: students in the Common First preparatory year at King Saud University, Riyadh; a randomly selected sample of 374 was emailed a Google form; 282 participated, response rate 75.4%; 63% female. Sample size target 267 (Raosoft, 5% margin of error, 90% confidence), inflated for an expected 30% non-response. Each participant was asked for up to three Arabic-language health-related WhatsApp messages that they or a relative had recently read; average 1.2 messages per student; exact duplicates and non-health messages excluded, leaving 326 messages. Coding: four board-certified family/internal medicine consultants; two independent reviews per message against available scientific evidence; disagreements resolved by consensus of the remaining two reviewers, blinded to the first decision. Inter-rater reliability with Kappa was explicitly NOT calculated. Analysis in SPSS 22 with chi-square/Fisher's exact tests. Authors' own limitations: single institution, one academic year, no participant demographics collected, WhatsApp only, results 'cannot be unduly generalized'.
